topics.title: Which is Greater? game/marathon
topics.text:
In this game/marathon (anybody know why they always call them marathons?), you post two numbers in maths. These numbers will be A and B. You have to figure out if A is greater than B, or B is greater than A, or if A is equal to B, or if they are two real numbers impossible to determine, or if one or both of them is not a real number. These five choices will be marked as (A), (B), (C), (D), (E). Here is what a problem would look like:



In this problem, A=90-(89*2) and B=-89. Which is greater?

(A) A>B

(B) A<B

(C) A=B

(D) it is impossible to determine

(E) it is impossible to determine because one or more of them is not a real number



The answer is (A). The problems should always be in this format. These will always be the exact choices to the problem. And the problem will always look like the format above, only the values of A and B can vary. But, since I made this marathon, I'm going to let things get a little more interesting.



In this problem, A = the distance that the circumcenter is from each of the vertices of any triangle ABC, and B = the distance that the incenter is from the sides of the same triangle ABC. Which is greater?

(A) A>B

(B) A<B

(C) A=B

(D) it is impossible to determine

(E) it is impossible to determine because one or more of them is not a real number.



The answer is (A). See the difference? Since I am taking an Introduction to Geometry class, I decided to get a little crazy and kick in some geometry into this greater than game. Well, what are you waiting for? Go make up some problems and post them here!

topics.title: Topic on 1+2+3+4 Repeating
topics.text:
Hey guys,

So I just wanted to share my opinions on the $1+2+3+4+5\ldots$ that everyone has either gotten hyped or mad about.

In this thread, please do not fight and if you disagree, do so politely.

This is my opinion on the thread.

I do not believe that $1+2+3+4+5\ldots$ is equal to $-1/12$ or whatever it is.

For many people, and Numberphile, a youtube channel explains this, that they base the proof off of this one:

$1-1+1-1+1-1+1-1+1\ldots$ is equal to $1/2$.

This is where I first believe is incorrect. You cannot assume a value for this equation. It is ongoing. It never stops, so can't just average the list of numbers and be done with it. If I had a bunch of test grades with $87, 88, 87, 88,$ and so on, and this repeated, it would be like saying: the next test grade will be an $87.5$. It won't be. It would either be $87$ or $88$. Same goes for this equation. Also, take a moment to think about this. The 1st value was $1$. The 2nd was $0$. The 3rd is $1$, and ongoing. Notice how in our equation, never does $1/2$ ever appear in this equation. So why would you assume that the value for this equation is $1/2$? To be honest, I think a better solution would be $1$ or $0$, since they are the ones that fundamentally appear in the equation. Like I said above, if you disagree, please do politely.

Another backup that people say for this proof is that Numberphile said it, therefore, since it is credible, it is always right, such as: http://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c3h1530507p9202254

Wrong.

Almost any breakthrough in science or mathematics was disregarding credible sources. The mathematicians or scientists that made such breakthroughs said, "Wow, I think that is wrong. Let me research it and see if it is wrong or right." Take the Sun revolving Earth. Everyone thought that it was true since the church said so. And since the church was close to God, and God was always right, the church was right. That is practically what you guys are saying if you think Numberphile is credible. (Not saying it isn't, just a theory) Since some credible source said something, it's right. Once again, nothing would have been proven if we stuck to that philosophy.

Back to the math:

Note Djmathman's post about this topic. He/she explains it much better than I can, check it out there.

Here is another proof about the theory.

$1+2+3+4+5\ldots=-1/12$

Notice how the first value is $1$. The next is $3$. Then $6$. Are these numbers familiar?

They should be, if you know about Pascal's triangle.

The theory is that one specific row/column in the triangle holds the triangular numbers, being that $1+2+3+4+5\ldots$

is in the triangle. Yet if I went down in the row to the number that is infinitely down, I'm pretty sure that I would not find a number that is less than 0. Yet we know that the numbers are increasing in an exponential/periodic way that there is proof in the triangle. So why would you think that the number would be less than $0$, being $-1/12$?

Another proof:

This is fairly simple. All the values in the equation are integers. They will always be integers. Because the equation itself is made of integers, being $n+1$, $n+2$, etc... Since the first term is an integer, and we add another integer to it in the equation, the value must be an infinitely large integer, not some fraction.

Like I said, please be polite when posting. I would not like to see this thread to be locked.

topics.title: Number Theory Problems
topics.text:
Hey guys,

Can someone please give the solutions along with the explanation? I tried these problems but still couldn't figure them out.



1. For two natural numbers, n and m, the GCD of n and m is 6 and the LCM of n and m is 600.



a) What primes are included in the prime factorization of either n or m?



b) What is the minimum of the exponent of each of those primes in the factorizations of n and m?



c) What is the maximum of the exponent of each of those primes in the factorizations of n and m?



d) How many distinct pairs of positive integers are there which have a GCD of 6 and an LCM of 600?



2. Let m and n be two relatively prime natural numbers. If m has 12 positive divisors and n has 10 positive divisors, what is the product of the positive divisors of mn?



3. There are 2000 cells in a particular jail. The cells are numbered 1 through 2000 and each contains 1 inmate. One night, while all the inmates are asleep, a series of 2000 computer glitches occurs. First, the computer unlocks all the cells. Then the computer turns the locks of every evenly numbered cell (2, 4, 6...), relocking only those cells. The computer then turns the locks of every third cell (3, 6, 9...), locking those cells that were unlocked and unlocking those that had been relocked. The glitch goes on through the first 2000 natural numbers, where for each natural number n, the computer turns the locks of the cells that are multiples of n.



a) For a cell numbered m, which of the 2000 glitches affects that cell?



b) How many of the prisoners will awaken to unlocked cells?



4. m and n are positive integers such that the GCD of m and n has 5 divisors, and the LCM of m and n has 30 divisors. What is the greatest possible number of prime divisors that n could have?

Hello, the problem is:

[quote]A bag contains five chips numbered 2 through 6. Danya draws chips from the bag one at a time and sets them aside. After each draw, she totals the numbers on all the chips she has already drawn. What is the probability that at any point in this process her total will equal 10? So some number of subsets of the chips will sum to a total of 10. To determine these subsets, I basically just thought about it, and came up with the right answer ({2, 3, 5} or {4, 6}).
